content.title: Welcome to 'Championship Valley' and Phoenix's NCAA Women's Final Four
content.text: March 29, 2026, 5:00 a.m. MTThis marks the first time the Women's Final Four will be held in Arizona, adding to the region's extensive history of hosting major sporting events.ESPN plans its largest-ever production for a Women's Final Four, with coverage broadcast in over 200 countries.“Championship Valley.”It has a nice ring to it, don’t you think? Considering all the major national sporting events the greater Phoenix area has hosted and staged over the years, perhaps it should become Arizona’s official new moniker.I only wish I had thought of it first.The words, though, belong to Phoenix Mayor Kate Gallego, who used them perfectly when summing up what it means to the city to host the 2026 NCAA Women’s Final Four downtown on April 3 and 5 at Mortgage Matchup Center.“Championship Valley rises again,” Gallego said recently at the arena during the Women’s Final Four Tip Off news conference. “I’m so excited to welcome the Women’s Final Four to downtown Phoenix. … We are going to put on a great show. The national championship and incredible fun, fan-friendly activities for the whole family are coming to downtown Phoenix.“We do an incredible job at major events and I’m confident we will rise to the challenge. This will be the best Women’s Final Four.”“Championship Valley” has been home to four separate Super Bowls, including two since 2015, and in that time has also hosted the NFL Pro Bowl (2015), the college football national championship (2016), the NCAA Men’s Final Four twice (2017, 2024), the WNBA All-Star Game (2024) and just in January, the College Football Playoff semifinals (2026).Next February, the 2027 NBA All-Star Game is also coming to town.Beyond that, no major national sporting events are in the works other than the usual annual events – the Vrbo Fiesta Bowl at State Farm Stadium and the Rate Bowl at Chase Field in college football, the WM Phoenix Open at TPC Scottsdale in golf, NASCAR at Phoenix Raceway, NHRA drag racing at Firebird Motorsports Park and, of course, Major League Baseball spring training in the Cactus League.Plus, we’ve got our share of local professional teams such as the NBA’s Phoenix Suns, MLB’s Arizona Diamondbacks, NFL’s Arizona Cardinals, WNBA’s Phoenix Mercury, USL Championship league’s Phoenix Rising FC, the Indoor Football League’s Arizona Rattlers and of course, Arizona State athletics.We’ve basically got it all and sometimes, it can be a rather competitive business when it comes to attracting attention and the almighty sports dollar. Although future Super Bowls, Final Fours and All-Star Games aren’t expected anytime soon, it doesn’t mean they won’t come.“We’re looking out at the next 10 years, and we’ve got a nice healthy pipeline of potential events,” said Kyle Hedstrom, the executive vice president and chief operating officer of the Arizona Sports & Events Alliance. “I have confidence that within the next 10 years we’re going to be hopefully as full up as we can be.”ESPN touts Phoenix as its 'biggest Women’s Final Four'This is the first time the Women’s Final Four is coming to the Valley, but it probably won’t be the last if they do it right.“Time and time again we’ve shown that nobody hosts the biggest sporting events better than Arizona and the Women’s NCAA Final Four will be no different,” Arizona Governor Katie Hobbs said in a video statement played at the Tip Off news conference.Last year’s Women’s Final Four brought fans from all 50 states and 23 countries to Tampa, Florida, and total tournament attendance reached 351,777, the third largest all-time mark. It was the fourth straight year to top attendance of 315,000 and the 2025 championship game between UConn and South Carolina peaked at 9.9 million viewers, the third-largest audience since ESPN began its exclusive-rights agreement in 1996.More than 300 ESPN personnel will descend on downtown Phoenix supported by nine production trucks on site, a similar level to what the network deploys for the College Football Playoff. The Women’s Final Four will be broadcast in more than 200 countries worldwide, with ESPN producing more than 19 hours of combined studio and game coverage.“This will be the biggest Women’s Final Four we’ve ever produced in terms of technology and coverage,” said Meg Aronowitz, ESPN’S senior vice president of production.Women's basketball on a roll as Final Four hits PhoenixWomen’s basketball is proving its popularity with sustained audience expansion, and it shouldn’t be a surprise, according to Lynn Holzman, NCAA vice president of Women’s Basketball.“We continue to see this growth. It’s not new,” Holzman said. “We’ve been growing for a long period of time. Of course, there’s been this catapult forward over the last five years or so, and much of that can be attributed back to 2023 when we had the storylines around Angel Reese and Caitlin Clark.“What that tells us when I mention those names is, it is about our players and our coaches. That is the No. 1 thing out of the gate. With that then, we need to create these environments that fans of all ages are finding these connections to the players. What is it about their stories that compels me to want to be a part of this entire cultural phenomenon of women’s sports, of which women’s basketball is a preeminent leader within?”The biggest reason, Holzman says flatly, is because “they are damn good basketball players.” Players today are more skilled, more athletic and are quicker and stronger, she said.The strong connection between players at the college and WNBA level also cannot be overstated, Holzman said, noting that “whether it’s fashion or how they use social media,” the name, image and likeness efforts (NIL) have helped transform the women’s game overall and “meet fans where they are at.”According to the Arizona Sports & Events Alliance, the 2025 NCAA Women’s Tournament as a whole drove 22.2 million engagements on social media accounts. Just attending a single college women’s basketball game can help create new young fans, according to Arizona State coach Molly Miller.“What I’ve seen in arenas that I really love are the little boys and girls with Sharpies that are waiting for autographs in the tunnel,” Miller said before she and her Sun Devils were eliminated by Virginia in the NCAA First Four. “It’s the little girls that have the same hairstyle as some of our players.“I say that because I have a 9-year-old, Crosby, and her basketball team came to a game and Marley (Washenitz), one of our players, had her hair up in a bubble braid – she had her hair in a ponytail with little sections of hair ties. We played on a Saturday, the whole team came, and then on Sunday I went to Crosby’s game and their whole team had bubble braids. … These kids are getting exposure to inspire this next generation.”NCAA Women's Final Four future sitesThe women’s game is getting so popular and the demand for viewership and attendance so great, Holzman notes the Women’s Final Four will be held in a pair of domed facilities in 2028 (Lucas Oil Stadium in Indianapolis) and 2029 (the Alamodome in San Antonio) to accommodate larger crowds.In 2027, the event is in Columbus, Ohio, at Nationwide Arena, which holds just about 20,000 fans.So, enjoy the Women's Final Four while it’s here, folks.“We’re looking forward to three unforgettable basketball games and almost as important, we’re also looking forward to the larger impact the championship will have on our state,” said Jay Parry, CEO of the Phoenix Final Four Local Organizing Committee. “The Women’s Final Four will drive tourism and economic activity across Arizona.“It will create philanthropic benefit for many programs we’re doing in the community and shine a global spotlight on Arizona as a world-class destination, as a place to live, as a place to do business and of course, to host major, mega sporting events like the Women’s Final Four.”Will it return to Arizona one day? Probably. So, too, will other mega sporting events, including perhaps the NFL draft, and the Super Bowl.Don’t forget, we are “Championship Valley.”Reach McManaman atbob.mcmanaman@arizonarepublic.
